subject: surgery
title: Thyroglossal Cyst, Branchial Anomalies, and Sistrunk Operation

steps.tx: Representing over seventy percent of all congenital neck masses, a **thyroglossal cyst** arises from the incomplete obliteration and persistent epithelial remnants of the embryonic thyroglossal duct. During early organogenesis in the third to fourth gestational week, the thyroid primordium descends from the foramen caecum at the base of the tongue through the developing second branchial arch to reach its definitive position in the anterior lower neck, leaving a duct that normally atrophies by the eighth week.
steps.say: Thyroglossal duct cysts are the most common congenital neck masses, arising from remnants of the embryonic tract left as the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum to the lower neck.

nodes.label: Thyroid Primordium at Foramen Caecum
Descends Through Hyoid Primordium to Lower Neck
Normal Obliteration of Thyroglossal Duct by Week 8
Failure of Obliteration Leaves Epithelial Remnant
Secretory Mucus Accumulates Forming Thyroglossal Cyst

steps.tx: This smooth midline swelling sits just below the hyoid, the commonest address for a thyroglossal cyst in practice. Asking for **tongue protrusion** makes the mass climb, proving its stalk still tethers to the foramen caecum through the hyoid. That single bedside movement separates a thyroglossal cyst from a dermoid, which stays indifferent when the tongue comes out.
steps.say: A midline cyst climbing on tongue protrusion proves its thyroglossal stalk. A dermoid cyst would stay unmoved by the manoeuvre.

vis.alt: Midline infrahyoid thyroglossal cyst in the neck of a patient protruding the tongue
vis.caption: Midline infrahyoid thyroglossal cyst shown as the patient protrudes the tongue. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: A thyroglossal cyst presents as a smooth, rounded, nontender, cystic swelling in the anterior midline of the neck. Although it can arise anywhere along the descent pathway from the tongue base to the suprasternal notch, over sixty percent develop in the infrahyoid region. On physical examination, the cyst moves upward on deglutition because of its attachment to the pretracheal fascia. Uniquely, the mass **moves with tongue protrusion**, because its persistent embryonic stalk connects directly to the foramen caecum via the hyoid bone.
steps.say: Thyroglossal cysts present as smooth midline neck lumps. They move upward during swallowing and, uniquely, elevate on tongue protrusion because the tract attaches to the tongue base.

left.title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
points: Arises strictly in or near the anterior midline of the neck
Moves upward both during deglutition and on tongue protrusion
Attached to the body of the hyoid bone and tongue base
Epithelial lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar or squamoid

right.title: Branchial Cleft Cyst
points: Arises along the lateral neck at anterior border of upper SCM
Does not move on deglutition or on tongue protrusion
Remnant of second branchial apparatus (cervical sinus of His)
Lined by stratified squamous epithelium surrounded by dense lymphoid tissue

steps.tx: Before planning surgical excision of any midline neck swelling suspected of being a thyroglossal cyst, high-resolution ultrasonography of the neck is mandatory. The critical imaging objective is to confirm the presence of a **normal orthotopic thyroid gland** in its expected lower cervical bed. In one to two percent of individuals with a midline mass, the apparent thyroglossal cyst actually represents an ectopic thyroid gland, and inadvertent surgical removal would plunge the patient into lifelong severe athyreotic hypothyroidism.
steps.say: Preoperative ultrasound must confirm a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck. This prevents accidental excision of an ectopic thyroid gland masquerading as a thyroglossal cyst.

rows: High-Resolution Neck Ultrasound
Confirms presence of normal bilobed thyroid gland in lower neck
Mandatory step to rule out solitary ectopic thyroid tissue prior to resection
Thyroid Function Tests (TSH)
Documents baseline euthyroid, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid status
Identifies subclinical hypothyroidism in children with ectopic thyroid tissue
Radionuclide Thyroid Scintigraphy
Technetium-99m uptake localized strictly to the cervical thyroid
Indicated if neck ultrasound fails to convincingly identify a normal thyroid bed
Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology
Aspiration of mucinous fluid with squamoid and ciliated epithelial cells
Excludes rare thyroglossal duct carcinoma, predominantly papillary thyroid cancer

steps.tx: Simple enucleation or unroofing of a thyroglossal cyst suffers a prohibitive recurrence rate approaching fifty percent because microscopic epithelial side-branches arborize intimately through the hyoid bone. The definitive, curative operation is the **Sistrunk operation**, described by Walter Sistrunk. This procedure entails en bloc excision of the cyst, the central core of the hyoid bone body, and a wide one-centimetre muscular core of tissue surrounding the tract up to the foramen caecum, reducing recurrence to less than three percent.
steps.say: Simple cyst removal carries a fifty percent recurrence risk. The definitive Sistrunk operation excises the cyst, the central body of the hyoid bone, and a core of tongue base muscle.

nodes.label: Transverse Midline Incision Over Cyst
Mobilize Cyst Toward Inferior Hyoid Border
Resect Central 1 cm Body of Hyoid Bone En Bloc
Core 1 cm Cylinder of Tongue Base Muscle to Foramen Caecum
Definitive Resection Drops Recurrence Below 3%

steps.tx: Lateral congenital neck masses arise predominantly from anomalies of the branchial apparatus. A **branchial cyst** develops in over ninety-five percent of cases from incomplete obliteration of the second branchial cleft, specifically persistence of the embryonic cervical sinus of His. It presents as a smooth, painless, fluctuant, nontender lateral neck swelling located along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of its upper and middle thirds, just below the angle of the jaw.
steps.say: Branchial cysts arise from second branchial cleft remnants. They present as smooth, fluctuant lateral neck swellings along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

left.title: Second Branchial Cleft Cyst
points: Accounts for ninety-five percent of all branchial anomalies
Located at anterior border of upper sternocleidomastoid
Aspiration yields turbid yellow fluid rich in cholesterol crystals
Lined by stratified squamous epithelium with abundant lymphoid follicles

right.title: First Branchial Cleft Cyst
points: Accounts for one to four percent of branchial anomalies
Located intimately related to external auditory canal or parotid
Closely associated with branches of the facial nerve
May present with chronic purulent ear discharge and parotid swelling

steps.tx: This scan shows a smooth cystic mass hugging the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, just below the angle of the jaw. That address is classic for a **second branchial cyst**, left behind when the cervical sinus fails to obliterate. In an adult, the same picture still obliges exclusion of cystic nodal metastasis before congenital origin is accepted.
steps.say: A cyst along the anterior sternocleidomastoid border fits a second branchial cyst. Adult cases still require exclusion of cystic metastasis.

vis.alt: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showing a well-circumscribed cystic second branchial cleft cyst along the anterior sternocleidomastoid
vis.caption: Contrast CT showing a well-circumscribed cystic second branchial cleft cyst along the anterior sternocleidomastoid. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Diagnostic fine-needle aspiration of a branchial cyst yields characteristic thick, turbid, brownish fluid containing abundant desquamated epithelial cells and glittering **cholesterol crystals** on microscopic polarized light examination. In adults presenting with an apparent branchial cyst, clinicians must exercise extreme vigilance to exclude a cystic cervical lymph node metastasis from an occult oropharyngeal or papillary thyroid carcinoma, demanding thorough endoscopic inspection and p16 immunohistochemical evaluation.
steps.say: Aspiration of a branchial cyst reveals thick turbid fluid rich in cholesterol crystals. In adults, surgeons must rigorously exclude a cystic lymph node metastasis from hidden oropharyngeal cancer.

rows: Benign Branchial Cyst
Young adult, long history of fluctuating mass, cholesterol crystals on FNAC
Wall shows benign squamous lining with germinal center lymphoid stroma
Cystic Oropharyngeal Metastasis
Adult smoker or HPV positive, painless cystic lateral neck node
HPV p16-positive squamous carcinoma from occult tonsil or tongue base primary
Cystic Papillary Thyroid Node
Mid to lower lateral neck, cystic fluid contains thyroglobulin
Metastatic deposit from microcarcinoma in clinically normal thyroid gland

steps.tx: When a persistent tract communicates both externally with the skin and internally with the pharynx, it constitutes a **second branchial fistula**. The external opening is positioned along the lower third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The fistulous tract ascends through cervical subcutaneous tissue and platysma, pierces the deep cervical fascia, passes between the internal and external carotid arteries, crosses over the hypoglossal nerve, and opens internally within the supratonsillar fossa.
steps.say: A second branchial fistula opens externally at the lower border of the sternocleidomastoid and terminates internally in the tonsillar fossa, passing between the internal and external carotid arteries.

nodes.label: External Skin Orifice at Lower Anterior SCM
Ascends Subcutaneously Through Platysma
Passes Between Internal & External Carotid Arteries
Crosses Superficial to Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII)
Internal Orifice at Supratonsillar Fossa (Tonsil Bed)

steps.tx: Complete surgical extirpation of a second branchial fistula requires complete removal of the entire tract from the lower neck up to the pharyngeal tonsillar bed. To achieve safe exposure without creating an unsightly long longitudinal cervical scar, surgeons employ a **stepladder incision technique**. Two separate horizontal transverse skin crease incisions are made: one encircling the lower cutaneous orifice and a second higher incision over the carotid bifurcation, allowing safe dissection of the tract between major neurovascular structures.
steps.say: Excision of a branchial fistula requires complete tract removal up to the tonsillar fossa. A stepladder approach with two horizontal incisions achieves full exposure without an unsightly vertical scar.

nodes.label: Cannulate Tract with Lacrimal Probe or Methylene Blue
Elliptical Transverse Incision Around Cutaneous Fistula
Second Higher Horizontal Incision at Carotid Bifurcation
Tract Pulled Through Subcutaneous Tunnel from Below
